p1.caption: P1: the ranking can be bought. (a) the distribution of the rank gain $G$ over all 684 cells — $G=0$ (the protocol ranks the policy where its payoff puts it) in 210, $G>0$ in 474. (b) the same reading per game: the share of each game's 76 cells with $G>0$ stays between 50 and 55, so the effect is not an artefact of bidder count or auction family.

p2.caption: P2: the protocol is the lever. (a) the exact two-way decomposition of $G$ in each game, on a log scale: the protocol's mean square exceeds the population's in 9 of 9 games. (b) the two ratios a reader could compute — the mean-square ratio (the claim, 3.929x to 52.132x) and the sum-of-squares ratio, which is larger for the protocol by construction because the protocol factor has 19 levels against the population's 4.

p3.caption: P3 refuted: buyable rank and fragile rank are two properties. (a) per protocol, the share of its 36 cells that are fragile (grey) and gameable (dark) — the dark never escapes the grey, which is the dominance $G>0 \Rightarrow \tau<1$ with 0 counterexamples. (b) the containment in cells: 474 gameable strictly inside 564 fragile, leaving a band of 90 cells that are already misordered while nothing can be bought in them.
